transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-10-14
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Acme Head of Platform), Priya Singh (Acme ML Eng), Carlos Mendez (Acme Security), Aisha Nair (Acme PM)

Summary (auto):
Quick console walkthrough focused on usage analytics, per-route dashboards, and cost breakdown. Discussed hosted vs dedicated, reserved capacity pricing, and security/compliance needs (SOC2, audit logs, KMS). Agreed to share pricing, console recording, and sample workload for a pilot bench mark.

Topics:
- Overview of per-route usage analytics and per-model cost attribution
- Cost breakdown and batching/caching levers
- Routing policies and dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs
- Security (audit logs, KMS, VPC) and procurement timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we really appreciate you taking the time. Quick roll call, I'm Maya, AE on the account, Ethan's our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Jordan Lee: Hey Maya, Jordan here. We, uh, had a quick internal note, trying to see how Redwood would map to our API gateway and existing observability.
[00:18] Priya Singh: Priya, ML eng. Hi.
[00:20] Carlos Mendez: Carlos from security.
[00:22] Aisha Nair: Aisha, PM. Morning.
[00:24] Ethan Park: Ethan here, I'll do the console portion, walk through the analytics and cost views, and then we can get into questions and the deeper POC scope.
[00:34] Maya Chen: Great, goal for today is a focused walkthrough of our Console usage analytics and per-route dashboards, show how cost attribution works per-route and per-model, and go over next steps for a pilot. We have about 45 minutes. Sound good?
[00:44] Jordan Lee: Yep, sounds good. We're most interested in per-route cost breakdowns and being able to tie that to our product teams for chargeback. Also curious about alerting on regressions and quality metrics.
[00:55] Ethan Park: Excellent. I'll share my screen — shows Console — forgive any lags.
[01:10] Ethan Park: So on the left nav you'll see Usage > Routes. The routes table maps your API routes to model endpoints, and we've got token counts, average latency, p50/p95, and cost columns. Note that the cost column uses your pricing profile — for hosted customers it's our published rates, for dedicated we accept a reserved capacity rate.
[01:35] Priya Singh: Quick question, is that per-token cost broken out by generation vs embeddings? We have two teams doing both.
[01:42] Ethan Park: Yes, we separate by unit type. See the breakdown view — generation tokens, embed units, and also rerank or search calls. You can filter by model family and time window.
[01:53] Maya Chen: Another thing to call out is the per-route cost attribution supports custom tags so you can map to your internal cost centers, e.g. product-a, chat-bot-team. That helps with chargeback.
[02:04] Jordan Lee: Nice, that's helpful. Does it export to CSV or integrate with our billing dashboard?
[02:09] Ethan Park: CSV export is available; we also have a REST endpoint for programmatic pulls. We can push aggregated reports to S3 or BigQuery if you want.
[02:20] Aisha Nair: Could you show the cost breakdown view for a sample route?
[02:25] Ethan Park: Yep — clicking into /chat/process — here you can see tokens-by-phase graph (prompt vs completion), average tokens per request, and an estimated cost per 1M requests. We also surface batching and KV cache hit rates that feed into unit cost. For example, this route has a 38% cache hit rate — which reduced effective token spend.
[02:46] Priya Singh: That cache stat — is that KV cache per session or prefix cache? How accurate are those numbers?
[02:52] Ethan Park: Good question — the Console shows both prefix cache and KV cache metrics. There's a sample size caveat: if traffic is irregular, the hit rate can vary; we provide the confidence interval on the metric. The number shown is our telemetry-derived estimate from the serving runtime.
[03:08] Jordan Lee: On routing — if we set a latency SLO, can requests be routed to a cheaper model variant when latency is relaxed? We want automated fallback for cost savings but keep user-facing latency.
[03:18] Ethan Park: Absolutely — routing policies can be configured by priority: region, latency SLO, cost tiers. You can set a rule: attempt primary model, if queue depth or latency exceeds threshold, failover to a compatible quantized variant or a lower-cost model. The Console surface will simulate expected cost/latency tradeoffs for those policies.
[03:37] Carlos Mendez: For security, quick question — where are the audit logs stored and can we ship them to our SIEM?
[03:43] Maya Chen: Yes, audit logs are available from the Private control plane or the hosted control plane; we can stream them to your SIEM via secure syslog or S3 with encryption. We also support KMS customer-managed keys in Private setups.
[03:55] Carlos Mendez: Do you have SOC2 and ISO attestations? And is there per-route data retention configuration?
[04:02] Ethan Park: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 reports available. For hosted customers there's a retention policy default, but for Dedicated/Private you can configure retention per-route and we support longer retention for debugging windows. We'll send the compliance pack after the call.
[04:18] Jordan Lee: Walk me through a cost optimization example — say we have a high-traffic inference path for our chat feature, what lever do you recommend?
[04:25] Ethan Park: Typically three levers: batching, caching (prefix/KV), and model quantization/variant routing. In the console you'll get recommended batching window and sample latency tradeoff graphs. For example we recommended batching window of 10ms for that route which increased throughput by 1.8x and lowered per-token compute cost by ~35% while p95 remained within your SLO.
[04:46] Priya Singh: Is that automatic or manual? We don't want to cause latency spikes for tail requests.
[04:50] Ethan Park: We provide suggested configs and you can enable auto-tune for safe ranges. Auto-tune gradually adjusts and has rollback on metric regressions.
[04:59] Aisha Nair: On the pricing side, how do reserved capacity numbers show up in the console?
[05:05] Maya Chen: In Dedicated accounts, reserved capacity shows as committed units and the Console applies a discounted per-token rate. There's a billing view that simulates month-over-month savings based on your commit level and run-rate.
[05:18] Jordan Lee: We will likely start hosted, then move to dedicated if the math works. Can you show a scenario comparison?
[05:24] Ethan Park: Sure — Console has a 'Compare' pane. Here we model a 30-day traffic shape — peak at 800 rps, steady 200 rps, average token length 120 — switching to Dedicated reduces per-token cost from $0.00028 to $0.00016 under a 3-month commit, showing 41% savings. The model factors in GPU utilization, batching effects, and KV cache efficacy.
[05:51] Priya Singh: There was previously mention of function/tool calling and structured outputs — do those change cost behavior?
[05:57] Ethan Park: Function calls are billed based on the model tokens used for the call; if you do many small tool calls, overhead can add up. We show an itemized view: model compute tokens, tool-call overhead, and any downstream embedding costs.
[06:12] Jordan Lee: What about multi-region routing — our app is global, can we pin certain customers to region for data residency?
[06:18] Ethan Park: Yes, routing policies support region pinning for compliance. We also surface region-level latencies and cost differences — sometimes a region has higher spot GPU pricing which affects per-token compute cost.
[06:28] Carlos Mendez: Can we encrypt request payloads server-side with our KMS?
[06:31] Maya Chen: For Private, yes — customer-managed KMS/HSM. For hosted we support envelope encryption with customer keys in some tiers; we'll follow up with exact options in the compliance pack.
[06:43] [07:00] Ethan Park: Quick demo continues — navigating to Alerts > Quality. Here you can wire evals and prompt sets to generate regression alerts tied to prompt-level metrics. If a model upgrade causes a drop in accuracy for a golden prompt set, it can trigger a rollback.
[07:20] Priya Singh: Can we hook that into our PagerDuty?
[07:22] Ethan Park: Yep, alerts can post to PagerDuty, Slack, or webhook endpoints.
[07:27] Aisha Nair: About the pilot — what does a typical pilot look like timeline-wise?
[07:31] Maya Chen: Typical POC is 2–6 weeks: week 0 onboarding and small traffic mirroring, week 1–2 run benchmarks and calibrate batching, week 3+ ramp to production traffic or run parallel (shadow) traffic, then decide on Dedicated commit. We'll tailor it to your needs.
[07:49] Jordan Lee: For the benchmark, we want to compare latency and cost with our in-house infra and with OpenAI — can Redwood run bench marks with our sample traffic?
[07:59] Ethan Park: Yes, we can run a controlled benchmark. We'll need a sample workload and an access window; we can provide a spreadsheet that maps metrics (p50/p95, tokens, cost per 1M requests). I'll share the benchmark template.
[08:12] Priya Singh: There are a couple of smaller details — can we limit who in our org can create routes or change routing policies? We need RBAC.
[08:19] Ethan Park: RBAC is supported — roles for Viewer, Operator, Admin, and custom roles. The Console shows exactly who changed route configs in the audit trail.
[08:31] Carlos Mendez: On SSO — does Redwood support SAML and SCIM provisioning?
[08:35] Maya Chen: Yes we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. We'll send SSO setup docs.
[08:44] Jordan Lee: Any hidden costs — for example, data egress or logging fees?
[08:48] Maya Chen: Standard egress charges apply for large downstream traffic in hosted setups, and optional additional cost for log retention beyond the included window. We'll call those out in the pricing sheet.
[08:58] Priya Singh: Back to the console — can you demo the per-route drilldown to show the last 24h activity?
[09:04] Ethan Park: Sure — filter route = /chat/process, timeframe = last 24 hours. You can see request volume by minute, heatmap of token distribution, and which model variants served traffic. There's a 'Top consumers' section showing which API keys or client ids generated the most cost.
[09:23] Jordan Lee: Client ids — we can use that for internal chargeback tagging. Great.
[09:27] Ethan Park: Also note the anomaly detection pane — if tokens per request spike, it will flag the route.
[09:34] Aisha Nair: For go/no-go on Dedicated, what are the typical procurement blockers?
[09:38] Maya Chen: Procurement usually focuses on contract SLA, data residency, and support SLAs. Security teams look at SOC2/ISO, encryption, and network controls (private subnet/VPC). We have enterprise contract addendums and can support custom SLAs.
[09:52] Carlos Mendez: We'll need to run your SOC2 and pen test artifacts by our security team.
[09:56] Maya Chen: Understood, we'll attach the compliance pack and a contact for security review.
[10:01] Jordan Lee: Quick question on integration — our current routing is through Kong/Gateway — is there an SDK or direct API we call?
[10:07] Ethan Park: You can call Redwood with standard REST/HTTP or gRPC. We provide SDKs (Python, Node) and a small sidecar example to integrate with Kong.
[10:16] Priya Singh: Does the SDK expose streaming responses and function/tool calling?
[10:19] Ethan Park: Yes, streaming via SSE/websocket and function call wiring is supported in the SDKs.
[10:24] Jordan Lee: About the demo notes you mentioned earlier, where will you host the console screenshots and the cost model?
[10:29] Maya Chen: We'll share a recording link and a Google Sheet cost model — I'll put both in the follow-up email. Ethan will include the console exports.
[10:36] Ethan Park: Quick digression — we also have Optimize suggestions in Console under 'Cost Insights' where we automatically surface quantization candidates and batching suggestions per route. This is powered by historical telemetry, so it's route-specific.
[10:52] Priya Singh: How aggressive are the quantization recommendations? We want to avoid quality regressions.
[10:56] Ethan Park: Recommendations come with an expected quality delta and a test harness. You can apply quantization to a shadow variant and run evals against golden prompts; the Console will show pass/fail thresholds.
[11:08] Aisha Nair: Any references to shared docs?
[11:10] Maya Chen: Yes, shared artifacts: Deck - https://redwood.app/share/console-walkthrough-deck (note: placeholder), Benchmark template - https://redwood.app/share/benchmark-template.xlsx.
[11:20] Jordan Lee: That should do it on content. A few last questions from security — encryption at rest, key rotation cadence?
[11:26] Ethan Park: Rotation is supported; for private deployments you control rotation cadence via your KMS. For hosted we rotate keys and provide proof of rotation in compliance pack.
[11:37] Carlos Mendez: Great. Timeline-wise, procurement will likely want a 3–6 week POC then decision. Any objections?
[11:44] Maya Chen: That aligns with our standard POC. We'll scope a 3-week pilot, run benchmarks, and reconvene.
[11:50] Jordan Lee: Ok. Next steps recap?
[11:52] Maya Chen: Recap — Maya to send pricing + contract sketch and compliance pack by Friday 2025-10-17; Ethan to share console recording, dashboard exports, and benchmark template by 2025-10-15; Acme to provide sample traffic profile and security contact by 2025-10-20. We'll tentatively book a follow-up for 2025-10-22 to review bench results.
[12:12] Priya Singh: Sounds good, thanks.
[12:14] Aisha Nair: Thanks everyone.
[12:15] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email.

End of transcript.
